title: Mining recalcitrant soil phosphorus (P) contributes to Spartina alterniflora invasion along the Chinese coast
content:

Abstract

Spartina alterniflora ranks among the most consequential invasive species in coastal wetlands globally; however, the adaptive strategies enabling its success under relatively phosphorus (P)-limited conditions remain poorly understood. As nutrient bioavailability fundamentally constrains invasion success, soil P bioavailability constitutes a key determinant of plant growth and reproductive output in coastal wetland ecosystems. We conducted a large-scale comparative survey across 25 coastal wetlands spanning nearly 20° of latitude in the native range of this species (North America, 27–43° N) and its typical invaded range (China, 20–39° N), employing a sequential biologically based phosphorus (BBP) fractionation method and trait–environment analyses Our results revealed, firstly, the total soil P content in invaded habitats was approximately 35% lower than that in native ranges and was dominated by recalcitrant mineral-bound HCl-P (accounting for 84% of the total BBP-extracted P), whereas native-range soils were rich in labile and moderately labile P fractions. Secondly, this shift in soil P pools was associated with a fundamental change in the plant P-acquisition strategy: S. alterniflora may employ a ‘P-mining’ strategy, effectively mobilizing recalcitrant HCl-P in invaded habitats. Thirdly, unlike native populations, which tend to allocate more of the acquired P to vegetative growth, the invaded populations appear to preferentially invest the mobilized P to sexual reproduction. This was evidenced by strong positive correlations between seed set and both CaCl2-P and HCl-P, while vegetative growth showed minimal response. Moreover, this P-allocation pattern intensified along the latitudinal gradient. These findings uncover a shift from using more labile P to mining recalcitrant P, consistent with a potential ‘P-mining for reproduction’ strategy contributing to the invasion success of S. alterniflora in relatively nutrient-poor wetlands. This adaptive nutrient acquisition and -use mechanism highlights how S. alterniflora potentially reshapes coastal P cycling and contributes to ecosystem transformation under ongoing global environmental changes, including nutrient limitation and biological invasion.
